title: Basics of German Language
summary: German alphabet, pronunciation rules, greetings, farewells, basic phrases, and self-introduction.

exam_protocols.sprechen_teil_1: Crucial for the self-introduction. You must state your Name, Age, Country, Residence, and Profession. The examiner will definitely ask you to spell your name ('buchstabieren').

grammar_algorithms.logic: Long sound if followed by 1 consonant or 'H'. Short sound if followed by 2 consonants.
'ei' sounds like 'eye'. 'ie' sounds like 'ee'. 'eu/äu' sounds like 'oy'.
'w'=English 'v'. 'v'=English 'f'. 'st/sp' at start='sht/shp'. 'z'='ts'.
At start/middle: S sounds like Z. At end or doubled: S sounds like English S.
grammar_algorithms.formula: S start/middle = Z | S end/doubled = S

grammar_algorithms.logic: Ä = 'ay' in 'may'. Ö = 'er' with rounded lips. Ü = 'ue' with rounded lips.

turns.english: Hello, my name is Thomas. What's your name?

turns.english: Hello, I am Julia. I come from Germany.

turns.english: I come from England. I live in Berlin.

turns.speaker: B

title: Articles, Nouns & The Gender Engine
summary: Definite and indefinite articles, noun gender rules by suffix, compound nouns, days and months.

exam_protocols.lesen_teil_2: Crucial for Reading Part 2. Ads often use compound nouns. Applying the 'Compound Nouns' logic helps you instantly identify the core object being sold or rented.

grammar_algorithms.logic: der (masculine), die (feminine), das (neutral), die (plural).
ein (masculine/neutral), eine (feminine). No indefinite plural exists.
Endings: -ig, -ling, -or, -ismus. Categories: Days, Months, Seasons, Directions.
Endings: -ung, -heit, -keit, -tät, -ion, -ik, -ie, -e (mostly). Numbers are always feminine.
Endings: -chen, -lein, -ment, -um. Colors and metals are neutral.
The article ALWAYS comes from the LAST word in the compound.
examples: das Wasser + die Flasche = die Wasserflasche
der Fuß + der Ball = der Fußball

title: Pronouns, Numbers, Dates & The Plural Vault
summary: Personal pronouns, singular vs plural nouns, numbers 0-1M, phone numbers, ordinal numbers, dates.

exam_protocols.hören_teil_1: Listen carefully to numbers. Phone numbers and prices are always tested (e.g., 'null-eins-fünf...').
exam_protocols.sprechen_teil_1: You must be able to state your exact age, phone number, and birthday utilizing ordinal numbers.

grammar_algorithms.logic: Read backwards: Unit + und + Ten.
1-19: add '-te'. 20+: add '-ste'. Exceptions: erste (1st), dritte (3rd), siebte (7th).
Masculine often adds '-e'. Feminine often adds '-en'. Neutral often adds '-er'. Words ending in -er/-el often only change article.

title: Sentence Structure, Negation & Time
summary: Basic sentence structure, verb position (Position 2 rule), present tense conjugation, sein/haben, negation, telling time, ordering and paying.

exam_protocols.schreiben_teil_2: When writing your email, NEVER violate the Golden Rule: The conjugated verb MUST sit in Position 2.
exam_protocols.hören_teil_1: Telling time is heavily tested. Look out for the informal 'halb' (halfway to the next hour) and 'viertel'.

grammar_algorithms.logic: The conjugated verb MUST always be in Position 2. Position means phrase, not word. Subject is usually Pos 1 or 3.
In a main clause (Hauptsatz), the Subject comes directly BEFORE or AFTER the verb.
'kein' negates indefinite nouns (replaces ein). 'nicht' negates verbs, adjectives, and definite nouns.
'Halb' + NEXT hour (8:30 = halb neun). Use 'vor' (to) and 'nach' (past).
Remove -en from infinitive to get stem. Add endings: -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en.
examples: spielen: ich spiele, du spielst, er spielt, wir spielen, ihr spielt, sie spielen

grammar_algorithms.logic: In present tense, only 2nd and 3rd person singular change stem. Changes: e→i, e→ie, a→ä.
grammar_algorithms.formula: Only du/er change: e→i | e→ie | a→ä

turns.speaker: A
turns.english: I would like to order please.

turns.speaker: B
turns.english: What would you like to drink?

turns.speaker: A
turns.english: I would like to pay please.

title: Questions & Time Prepositions
summary: Yes/No questions, W-questions, time prepositions (am/um/im), weather vocabulary, seasons, extended introduction.

exam_protocols.sprechen_teil_2: You will pull a card with a topic (e.g., 'Wochenende') and must formulate a W-Question or Yes/No Question. Use the W-Question Algorithm.
exam_protocols.hören_teil_2: Crucial for identifying dates and times in announcements. Listen carefully for 'am' (days) vs. 'um' (exact time).

grammar_algorithms.logic: The conjugated verb moves to Position 1. The subject immediately follows.
examples: Lernst du Deutsch? (Are you learning German?)

grammar_algorithms.logic: W-word sits at Position 1, followed by the conjugated verb at Position 2, then the subject.
Different times require specific prepositions. 'um' (exact time), 'am' (days/dates), 'im' (months/seasons), 'gegen' (around a time), 'von...bis' (from...to), 'ab' (from [time] onwards).
grammar_algorithms.formula: um=time | am=days | im=months/seasons | gegen=approx time | ab=onwards

grammar_algorithms.concept: Location vs Direction Questions (wo / woher / wohin)
grammar_algorithms.logic: 'woher' = from where (origin). 'wo' = where (static location). 'wohin' = where to (direction/destination).
grammar_algorithms.formula: woher = origin | wo = static | wohin = destination
examples: Woher kommst du? (From where do you come?)
Wo wohnst du? (Where do you live?)
Wohin gehst du? (Where are you going?)

title: Adjectives, Colors & The Description Engine
summary: Adjective usage, adjective endings in Nominative (definite, indefinite, no article), modifiers, and colors.

exam_protocols.lesen_teil_2: Hack: Pay close attention to adjectives in ads (e.g., 'ein kleines Apartment'). If your prompt says you have a large family, eliminate the 'kleines' option immediately.
exam_protocols.sprechen_teil_2: Crucial for describing favorite items (e.g., 'Mein Lieblingsauto ist rot').

grammar_algorithms.logic: When an adjective simply describes the subject and comes AFTER verbs like sein/werden/bleiben, it does NOT change. It remains in its dictionary form.
When an adjective is placed DIRECTLY BEFORE a noun with der/die/das, it must mutate to reflect the noun's gender.
When used with ein/eine/ein, the adjective ending takes on the primary gender marker.
'Sehr' (very) is used for positive praise. 'Zu' (too) implies negative excess.

a1_adjective_pairs.example: Das ist sehr wichtig für mich.

title: Modal Verbs, Separable Verbs & The Sandwich Rule
summary: Modal verbs (können, müssen, wollen, sollen, dürfen, mögen), separable verbs, daily routines, and forming questions with modals.

exam_protocols.schreiben_teil_2: Essential for formulating intents in your email (e.g., 'Ich muss arbeiten' or 'Ich will kommen').
exam_protocols.sprechen_teil_3: The entire 'Bitten' (Requests) section requires you to formulate polite requests using modals: 'Können Sie mir bitte helfen?'

grammar_algorithms.logic: The conjugated modal verb locks into Position 2. The main verb gets kicked to the absolute END of the sentence and remains in its infinitive form.
grammar_algorithms.formula: Subject + [Conjugated Modal Pos 2] + Object/Info + [Infinitive Main Verb END]

grammar_algorithms.logic: Exam Hack: For ALL modal verbs, the 'ich' form and the 'er/sie/es' form are EXACTLY identical. Memorize one, use it for both.
The prefix splits off and moves to the very END of the sentence. UNLESS used with a Modal Verb, then the prefix and base verb rejoin as an infinitive at the end.
grammar_algorithms.formula: Simple: Prefix to END | With Modal: Joined infinitive to END
examples: Ich stehe um 7 Uhr auf. (Prefix at end)
Ich muss um 7 Uhr aufstehen. (Joined with modal)

grammar_algorithms.logic: If the prefix itself has a standalone meaning in German (mit, an, auf, zu), the verb is separable. If the prefix has no meaning (be-, er-, ver-), it is inseparable.
In W-Questions, the Modal is at Pos 2. In Yes/No questions, the Modal is at Pos 1. The Main verb ALWAYS stays at the end.

title: Past Tense (Präteritum)
summary: Simple past of haben and sein, regular/irregular Präteritum, transportation vocabulary, making appointments, and apologizing.

exam_protocols.schreiben_teil_2: Extremely useful for emails explaining a past event: 'Ich war in Berlin' or 'Ich hatte keine Zeit'.

grammar_algorithms.logic: Irregular but essential. Used constantly in everyday speech. Ich = er/sie/es (war).
grammar_algorithms.formula: ich war | du warst | er war | wir waren | ihr wart | sie waren

grammar_algorithms.logic: Also commonly used in speech. Ich = er/sie/es (hatte).
grammar_algorithms.formula: ich hatte | du hattest | er hatte | wir hatten | ihr hattet | sie hatten

grammar_algorithms.logic: Take the verb stem, add '-te', then the personal ending. If stem ends in 'd' or 't', add an extra 'e' (-ete).
examples: machen → ich machte, du machtest, er machte

title: The Perfect Tense & Housing
summary: Perfekt construction, Partizip II formation (regular/irregular/separable), haben vs. sein decision engine, apartment vocabulary.

exam_protocols.schreiben_teil_2: Mandatory for writing about the past in your email. Exams almost always ask 'Was hast du am Wochenende gemacht?' Use the Perfekt tense to respond.
exam_protocols.hören_teil_3: Listen carefully for 'ge-' words on answering machine messages to identify the main action the caller took.

grammar_algorithms.logic: Position 2 holds the conjugated helper verb (haben or sein). The past participle (Partizip II) is locked at the absolute END of the sentence.
grammar_algorithms.formula: Subject + [Helper Verb Pos 2] + Info + [Partizip II END]

grammar_algorithms.concept: Helper Verb Decision Engine (haben vs. sein)
grammar_algorithms.logic: Use 'sein' ONLY IF the verb shows Movement (A to B) OR a Change of State (waking up, dying) OR the verbs sein/bleiben/werden. Use 'haben' for 90% of all other actions.
grammar_algorithms.formula: sein = movement/state change | haben = everything else
examples: Ich bin nach Berlin gefahren. (sein - movement)
Ich habe Deutsch gelernt. (haben - no movement)

grammar_algorithms.logic: Add 'ge-' to the front and '-t' to the end. If stem ends in d/t, add '-et'.
grammar_algorithms.formula: ge + stem + t | ge + stem(d/t) + et

grammar_algorithms.logic: Verbs ending in '-ieren' NEVER take 'ge-'.
The 'ge-' is placed BETWEEN the prefix and the base verb.

title: Accusative Case & Professions
summary: Accusative articles, accusative pronouns, adjective endings in accusative, negation with keinen, professions.

exam_protocols.lesen_teil_2: Crucial for identifying exactly what someone needs in an advertisement ('Er sucht *einen* Job').
exam_protocols.sprechen_teil_3: When pulling a card, you must use accusative to ask for the item: 'Ich brauche *einen* Stift'.

grammar_algorithms.logic: ONLY the masculine gender changes. der→den, ein→einen, kein→keinen. Feminine, Neutral, and Plural stay the same.
Subject (Nominativ) = WHO does action. Object (Akkusativ) = WHAT receives action.
grammar_algorithms.formula: Who verb? = Subject | What gets verbed? = Object
examples: Der Hund sieht die Katze (Hund=subject, Katze=object)

grammar_algorithms.logic: After the verb 'sein', always use Nominativ (not Akkusativ). The second noun defines the subject.
examples: Das ist ein guter Mann (NOT: einen guten Mann)

grammar_algorithms.logic: Same as Nominativ EXCEPT masculine: definite→-en, indefinite→-en.
grammar_algorithms.formula: Masculine Akk: always -en | Rest: same as Nom
examples: Ich sehe die schöne Frau (-e, no change)

grammar_algorithms.logic: Pronouns change when they are the direct object.
grammar_algorithms.mapping: ich→mich, du→dich, er→ihn, sie→sie, es→es, wir→uns, ihr→euch, Sie→Sie

title: Possessive Articles & Clothing
summary: Possessive articles (mein, dein, sein...) in Nominative and Accusative, clothing vocabulary.

exam_protocols.sprechen_teil_1: During self-introduction, expect questions like 'Wie ist *Ihre* Telefonnummer?' Know your possessives.
exam_protocols.hören_teil_1: Listen for the mutated plural noun endings to distinguish if someone bought one item or multiple.

grammar_algorithms.logic: Used WITH a noun. They take the same endings as the indefinite article 'ein/eine/ein'.
grammar_algorithms.roots: ich→mein, du→dein, er/es→sein, sie→ihr, wir→unser, ihr→euer, sie/Sie→ihr/Ihr

grammar_algorithms.logic: Possessives follow the same endings as 'ein'. Accusative masculine: add -en.
examples: Nominativ: mein Hund, meine Katze, mein Buch
Akkusativ: meinen Hund, meine Katze, mein Buch

grammar_algorithms.logic: Articles sit WITH the noun (mein Auto). Pronouns REPLACE the noun and take the gender's ending (Das ist meins).
examples: Ist das dein Auto? Ja, das ist meins.

title: Dative Case & Directions
summary: Dative articles, dative pronouns, dative verbs, location vs direction (Wo/Wohin), two-way prepositions, giving directions.

exam_protocols.hören_teil_2: Crucial for navigating train stations. Listen for Dative contractions like 'am Bahnhof' or 'am Gleis 3'.
exam_protocols.schreiben_teil_2: When arranging meetings via email, you must use Dative for static locations: 'Wir treffen uns am Bahnhof.'

grammar_algorithms.logic: ALL genders mutate in Dative. It represents the indirect object/beneficiary, or a static location.
grammar_algorithms.formula: m/n: der/das→dem | f: die→der | pl: die→den(+n)

grammar_algorithms.logic: ein(m/n) → einem. eine(f) → einer.
Static location (Wo?) = Dative. Movement/direction (Wohin?) = Accusative.
examples: Wo bist du? Im Park (Dative - location)
Wohin gehst du? In den Park (Accusative - direction)

grammar_algorithms.logic: 'nach' (Cities/Countries without articles), 'zu' (Local places/people - always Dative), 'in' (Entering enclosed spaces - Accusative).

title: Comparisons & Shopping
summary: Comparative and superlative forms, demonstrative pronouns (dieser/diese/dieses), grocery shopping vocabulary, frequency adverbs.

grammar_algorithms.logic: Adjective + -er + 'als'. Many common adjectives get umlaut (a→ä, o→ö, u→ü).
'am' + adjective + '-sten'. Adjectives ending in -t/-d/-s/-z add '-esten'.
'dieser/diese/dieses' = 'this (specific)'. Endings follow definite article pattern.

title: Imperative (Commands) & Exam Survival
summary: Imperative mood (commands) for du/ihr/Sie, body parts, health vocabulary, doctor appointments.

exam_protocols.sprechen_teil_3: This section is entirely based on the Imperative. ALWAYS add 'bitte' (please) to secure full points for politeness.
exam_protocols.survival_hack_1: If you don't know an item on the card, say: 'Das Wort kenne ich nicht, was bedeutet das?'
exam_protocols.survival_hack_2: If you freeze or don't understand the examiner, DO NOT say 'Keine Ahnung'. Say: 'Wie bitte? Ich habe Sie nicht richtig verstanden.'

grammar_algorithms.logic: Conjugated verb + Sie. Same as question form but with exclamation.
Verb stem only (drop -st ending, no pronoun). Verbs with e→i keep the change. Verbs with a→ä lose the umlaut.
grammar_algorithms.formula: Verb stem (no -st, no du) | e→i stays | a→ä drops

grammar_algorithms.logic: Same as normal ihr-conjugation, but without the pronoun.
Prefix still goes to the end, even in imperative.
Three verbs don't follow the standard rules: haben, sein, werden.
grammar_algorithms.sein_rule: du: Sei! | ihr: Seid! | Sie: Seien Sie!
grammar_algorithms.haben_rule: du: Hab! | ihr: Habt! | Sie: Haben Sie!
grammar_algorithms.werden_rule: du: Werde! | ihr: Werdet! | Sie: Werden Sie!
